This is crucial for accurate studies on grid stability, fault response, and protection setting validation; however, the computational burden is substantial, as simulating a 70-MW system (with 22 IT load domains and 8 cooling domains), each with unique electrical devices (with controls and measurements), requires significant central processing unit time, memory, and data management efforts. 21 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. • Aggregate modeling offers a practical alternative by reducing the model complexity through lumping similar devices, enabling more rapid simulations that are suitable for high-level scenario planning or grid impact studies—for example, lumping the IT racks with UPS, which are spread over several rows, into a single IT load with a large inline UPS. • A hybrid approach is often effective, employing detailed modeling for critical components (e.g., BESS, UPS, critical transformers) while aggregating less critical or more uniform loads (e.g., bulk IT and cooling loads) to optimize fidelity and efficiency trade-offs. 22 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 6 Conclusion This framework provides a structured, modular approach for representing data center power systems within EMT platforms such as PSCAD or a digital real-time simulator. By integrating component-level dynamics, protective coordination, and high-level control logic, it captures both transient and steady-state behavior under abnormal grid events. The inclusion of grid-following, grid-forming, and black-start capabilities ensures applicability across evolving data center architectures. Aligning with recent reliability observations, the framework enables NERC and utilities to assess aggregate load behavior at the POI, identify vulnerability thresholds, and support the development of standards for reliable large load integration. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
